Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- A well-known Iranian filmmaker has written an open letter calling for the release of journalist Roxana Saberi. In a letter, Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi blames himself for urging Roxana Saberi to stay in Iran. Bahman Ghobadi said he kept quiet about the arrest and conviction of the Iranian-American journalist at the request of her family. After Saberi was convicted last weekend and sentenced to an eight-year prison sentence, he said he felt he had to do something. He told CNN that Saberi, whom he described as his fiancee, is caught in a "game of politics." In his letter, which has been posted by the International Campaign for Human Rights in Iran, Ghobadi blames himself for urging Saberi to stay in Iran despite her desire to leave. Also, he writes, "My letter is a desperate call to all statesmen ... and to all those who can do something to help." "From the other side of the ocean, the Americans have protested against her imprisonment, because she is an American citizen," he writes. "But I say no, she is Iranian, and she loves Iran. I beg you, let her go! I beg you not to throw her in the midst of your political games! She is too weak and too pure to take part in your games. Let me be present at her trial, sit next to her wise father and gentle mother, and testify she is without guilt or reproach." The 40-year-old filmmaker said that Saberi was planning to leave the country, but he kept her from leaving until his latest film -- which will be shown at this year's Cannes film festival -- was completed. Ghobadi won the 2000 Golden Camera award at the Cannes festival for his feature film, "A Time for Drunken Horses." Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison after a one-day trial that was closed to the public. The decision prompted sharp denunciations from President Barack Obama, as well as other U.S. and international officials. Iranian officials initially said Saberi was held for buying a bottle of wine. The Foreign Ministry later said she was detained for reporting without proper accreditation. On April 9, word emerged that Saberi had been charged with espionage. Saberi's lawyer has said he will appeal the verdict. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi has ordered the head of Tehran's Justice Department to make sure the appeals process is quick and fair. Ghobadi wrote that he is "optimistic about her release, and I firmly hope the verdict will be canceled in the next stage of the trial." "My Iranian girl with Japanese eyes and an American ID, is in jail. Shame on me! Shame on us!" CNN's Igor Krotov and Shirzad Bozorghmehr contributed to this report.

Let me be present at her trial, sit next to her wise father and gentle mother, and testify she is without guilt or reproach.”

The 40-year-old filmmaker said Saberi had been planning to leave the country, but that he persuaded her to stay until his latest film — which is scheduled to be shown at this year’s Cannes Film Festival — was completed.

Ghobadi won the Golden Camera award at the 2000 Cannes Film Festival for his feature film, *A Time for Drunken Horses*.

Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison after a one-day trial that was closed to the public. The decision drew sharp denunciations from President Barack Obama, as well as from other U.S. and international officials.

Iranian officials initially said Saberi had been detained for buying a bottle of wine. The Foreign Ministry later said she had been held for reporting without proper accreditation. On April 9, reports emerged that Saberi had been charged with espionage.

Ghobadi wrote that he is “optimistic about her release, and I firmly hope the verdict will be canceled in the next stage of the trial.”

## Roxana Saberi, an Eight-Year Sentence, and Bahman Ghobadi’s Plea for Her Freedom

In 2009, the case of Roxana Saberi, an Iranian-American freelance journalist, became an international flashpoint over press freedom, due process, and Iran’s treatment of dual nationals. Saberi, who had reported from Iran for outlets including NPR, the BBC, and other international media, was arrested in Tehran and later sentenced to eight years in prison on charges of espionage—an accusation she denied.

Saberi had been living in Iran for several years while working as a journalist and researching a book. Iranian authorities initially said she had been detained for buying alcohol, which is illegal in the country. The case soon escalated, however, with prosecutors accusing her of spying for the United States. Her trial was held behind closed doors, and the resulting eight-year sentence drew swift condemnation from press-freedom organizations, human-rights advocates, and Western governments.

The sentence came at a politically sensitive moment, as the United States under President Barack Obama was signaling interest in a new diplomatic opening with Iran after decades of hostility. Saberi’s imprisonment threatened to become a major obstacle in that effort, while also highlighting broader concerns about Iran’s judiciary and the vulnerability of journalists working there.

Among the most emotional public appeals for Saberi’s release came from acclaimed Iranian Kurdish filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi, known internationally for films such as *A Time for Drunken Horses* and *Turtles Can Fly*. Ghobadi revealed that he and Saberi had a close personal relationship and described her as a gentle, intellectually curious person who loved Iran and its culture. In an open letter, he pleaded for compassion and justice, arguing that Saberi was not a spy but a journalist and writer who had devoted herself to understanding the country.

Ghobadi’s appeal was notable not only because of his prominence as a filmmaker, but because public advocacy in politically sensitive cases in Iran could carry risks. His letter personalized Saberi’s case, shifting attention from the abstract language of diplomacy and espionage allegations to the human cost of her detention. He portrayed her as someone caught in a political struggle far larger than herself and called on authorities to reconsider her sentence.

International pressure continued to build. The U.S. government called the accusations baseless and demanded her release, while organizations such as the Committee to Protect Journalists and Reporters Without Borders criticized the secrecy of the proceedings. Saberi reportedly went on a hunger strike while imprisoned in Tehran’s Evin Prison, further intensifying concern about her health.

In May 2009, an Iranian appeals court reduced Saberi’s sentence from eight years to a suspended two-year term, and she was released from prison after spending about 100 days in custody. She left Iran shortly afterward.

Saberi’s case remains one of the most prominent examples of the risks faced by journalists, dual nationals, and writers in Iran. It also stands as a moment when public pressure—from governments, rights groups, fellow journalists, and cultural figures like Bahman Ghobadi—helped turn an individual imprisonment into an international cause.

**Iranian-American journalist Roxana Saberi sentenced to eight years as international pressure mounts; filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi pleads for her release**

Roxana Saberi, an Iranian-American freelance journalist who had reported from Tehran for major international news organizations, became the focus of a widening diplomatic and human-rights dispute after Iranian authorities arrested her, tried her behind closed doors on espionage charges, and sentenced her to eight years in prison.

Saberi, who was born in the United States to an Iranian father and Japanese mother and grew up in North Dakota, had lived in Iran for several years while working as a journalist and researching a book. She had contributed reports to outlets including National Public Radio, the BBC, Fox News and other international media. Iranian authorities said her press credentials had expired, and early accounts of her detention suggested she had first been accused of relatively minor violations, including buying alcohol, which is illegal in Iran, and reporting without proper accreditation.

But the case quickly escalated. Iranian officials later accused Saberi of spying for the United States, an allegation her family, attorneys and U.S. officials strongly denied. Her father, Reza Saberi, traveled to Iran to support her and repeatedly said his daughter was not a spy and had been pressured while in custody. Supporters said the shifting accusations raised serious doubts about the case and suggested the charges were politically motivated.

Saberi was held in Tehran’s Evin Prison, a facility known for housing political detainees, journalists, student activists and dissidents. Her detention came at a tense moment in relations between Iran and the United States, shortly after President Barack Obama took office and publicly signaled interest in a new diplomatic opening with Tehran.

### Closed-door trial and eight-year sentence

In April 2009, Saberi was brought before an Iranian Revolutionary Court in a trial that was not open to the public. Her lawyer said the proceedings were brief. Soon afterward, Iranian authorities announced that she had been convicted of espionage and sentenced to eight years in prison.

The sentence drew immediate condemnation abroad. Critics said the case lacked transparency and that Saberi had not been given a fair opportunity to defend herself. Press-freedom organizations argued that the prosecution fit a broader pattern in which Iran’s security establishment treated independent journalism and contact with foreign institutions as suspicious or hostile activity.

The U.S. government responded sharply. President Obama said he was “deeply concerned” and stated that Saberi was not involved in espionage. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton called for her release, and U.S. officials asked Swiss diplomats—who represent American interests in Iran in the absence of formal diplomatic relations—to seek access and information. The case complicated tentative efforts by the Obama administration to engage Iran after decades of estrangement.

International news organizations, human-rights groups and press-freedom advocates also pressed Iran to release Saberi. Reporters Without Borders, the Committee to Protect Journalists, Human Rights Watch and others criticized the prosecution, saying it appeared to criminalize journalistic work and deny due process. The European Union and several governments expressed concern, and the case became a rallying point for advocates of detained journalists around the world.

### Hunger strike and family appeals

Saberi’s family said she began a hunger strike in prison to protest her conviction, further heightening concern over her health. Her father described emotional phone calls and said she was under great strain. Supporters feared that prolonged detention and isolation could damage her physically and psychologically.

Iranian officials gave differing accounts of her condition and the legal process. Some officials defended the conviction, while others indicated the case could be reviewed on appeal. Iran’s judiciary eventually said the sentence would be reconsidered, though it maintained that the matter was being handled according to Iranian law.

### Bahman Ghobadi’s open letter

One of the most emotional public appeals came from acclaimed Iranian Kurdish filmmaker **Bahman Ghobadi**, known internationally for films such as *A Time for Drunken Horses* and *Turtles Can Fly*. Ghobadi, who had a close personal relationship with Saberi, wrote an open letter to Iranian authorities pleading for her freedom.

In the letter, Ghobadi described Saberi not as a political operative or spy, but as a compassionate, intellectually curious journalist and writer who loved Iranian culture and had spent years trying to understand and explain the country. His tone was deeply personal and anguished. He wrote of her loneliness in prison, her dedication to her work, and the pain of seeing someone he cared for portrayed as an enemy of the state.

Ghobadi appealed to Iranian officials’ humanity, asking them to recognize Saberi’s innocence and release her. He suggested that her imprisonment was a grave mistake and said the case had caused needless suffering to her family and friends. The letter stood out because it was not merely a legal or diplomatic argument; it was a public expression of grief from an artist asking the state to show mercy.

His appeal added a cultural and emotional dimension to a case already under intense international scrutiny. Coming from a prominent Iranian filmmaker, the letter underscored that concern for Saberi was not limited to Western governments or foreign advocacy groups. It also resonated among artists, journalists and intellectuals who saw her prosecution as part of a broader climate of fear surrounding expression in Iran.

### A case with broad significance

Saberi’s arrest and conviction became a symbol of the risks faced by journalists working in Iran, particularly those with dual nationality or ties to foreign media. Iranian authorities do not recognize dual citizenship in the same way as the United States and often treat Iranian-born or Iranian-descended dual nationals as Iranian citizens subject solely to Iranian law. That position has frequently complicated consular access and international efforts to intervene in such cases.

The timing also amplified the case’s importance. Obama had used a Persian New Year message in March 2009 to call for a new beginning with Iran, addressing both the Iranian people and leadership. Saberi’s sentencing just weeks later placed a major obstacle in the path of any thaw, giving critics of engagement an example of Tehran’s continued hostility toward the United States and toward independent media.

For Iran, the case unfolded amid domestic political sensitivity ahead of the country’s June 2009 presidential election. Authorities were wary of foreign influence, and accusations of espionage were often used in cases involving journalists, academics and civil-society figures.

### Appeal and release

Following the outcry, Saberi’s case went to appeal. In May 2009, an Iranian appeals court reduced her sentence from eight years to a suspended two-year term, and she was released from Evin Prison. Her release was welcomed by her family, U.S. officials, press organizations and human-rights advocates, though many continued to criticize the original prosecution and the conditions under which she had been detained.

After leaving prison, Saberi departed Iran. She later spoke publicly about her ordeal, including the pressure she faced during interrogation and the emotional toll of imprisonment. Her case remained one of the most prominent examples of Iran’s detention of a dual-national journalist and continued to be cited in discussions of press freedom, due process and the use of national-security charges against writers and reporters.

For many observers, the image that endured was not only that of a journalist caught in a geopolitical struggle, but also the plea of Bahman Ghobadi—an artist’s open letter asking officials to look beyond accusation and power, and to free a woman he portrayed as innocent, humane and undeserving of prison.
